chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Ibrahim ibn Abi al-Bilad, who said:

I entered upon Abu Ja'far ibn al-Rida (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'I want to press my belly against your belly.' He said, 'Here, O Abu Ismail,' and he uncovered his belly. I uncovered my belly and pressed it against his. Then he seated me and called for a platter containing raisins, so I ate. Then he began speaking and complained to me about his stomach. I was thirsty, so I fetched water. He said, 'O Maid! Give him a drink from my nabidh.'

She brought me nabidh made from partially-ripened dates in a yellow cup. I drank it and found it sweeter than honey. I said to him, 'This is what spoils your stomach.' He said to me, 'These are dates from the charity of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). They are taken in the morning, water is poured over them, the maid soaks them, and I drink them after the meal and throughout the rest of my day. When it is night, the maid takes it and gives it to the people of the house to drink.'

I said to him, 'The people of Kufa are not satisfied with this.' He said, 'And what is their nabidh?' I said, 'They take the dates, clean them, and pour Al-Qa'wa over them.' He said, 'And what is Al-Qa'wa?' I said, 'Al-Daazy.' He said, 'And what is Al-Daazy?' I said, 'A grain brought from Basra, which is poured into this nabidh until it boils and intoxicates, then it is drunk.' He said, 'That is prohibited.'

key_terms.الدَّاذِيُّ: Al-Daazy: A grain brought from Basra used to induce intoxication in the drink.
key_terms.الْقَعْوَةُ: Al-Qa'wa: A specific ingredient or method used in preparing the Kufan nabidh.
key_terms.صَدَقَة: Sadaqah: Charity or alms, here referring to dates given to the Prophet.
key_terms.نَبِيذ: Nabidh: A drink made by soaking dates or raisins in water.

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the permissible nabidh of the Ahl al-Bayt and the intoxicating nabidh of the Kufans?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the Imam’s practical distinction between permissible *nabidh* and intoxicants by contrasting his method of consuming fresh, non-intoxicating date water with the Kufan practice of adding *Al-Daazy* (a grain from Basra) to induce intoxication. It underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the substance and preparation method as determinants for permissibility, linking the physical act of drinking to the spiritual state of sobriety. The narrative also illustrates the Imam’s generosity and the communal sharing of blessed sustenance, reinforcing the social dimension of dietary laws in early Islamic tradition.
